text:
The numbers settled. That’s all. Just settled. 

I’m done.

The lines were too neat. Too precise. It wasn’t the stone, not exactly. It was the subtraction. It felt… incomplete. Like a ledger entry that hadn’t quite settled. 

I wanted to stop. The collector, Haro, was a useless formality. The gate itself – that unsettling, sudden appearance – held the true weight. But the discrepancy… the single day missing in the ledger. It wasn't a debt, not yet. It was a question. And questions, especially when they came with no cost, felt like a trap. 

I wanted to keep reading. Not because I was invested in Wren's journey, not yet. But because that single missing day, that tiny imperfection in the system, was a fault line. Something was about to shift. The way the haze coalesced around the gate, the precise accounting of the toll – it all felt assembled, built on something not entirely honest. 

I pushed on.

It stopped. Just stopped. The syntax is too deliberate, too…precise. Like someone’s forcing a rhythm onto the words. The crate, the gate, the numbers – it’s all just a machine working. 

I want to know what's in that crate. Not because it’s exciting, not because it’s dangerous, but because the way this man, Haro, is treating it is *wrong*. The way he examines the seal, the way he insists on the “inspection,” the way he simply *writes* the figures down… it’s not about the toll. It’s about control. 

And the ledger. The meticulous, almost obsessive ledger entries. The discrepancy at the end of the last porter’s record. It’s not a mistake. It’s a seed. Something’s being tracked, deliberately, and the numbers aren’t adding up. 

I’m going to keep reading.

The rain was starting to fall, a fine, grey drizzle that didn’t seem to bother the crate or the gate. It bothered me. The numbers. The way they shifted, not just on the board, but in the ledger, in my own book. That one extra day – it wasn’t a mistake. It was… a key. 

I stopped reading. The System, the gate, Haro – it was all a carefully constructed illusion of order. And that one discrepancy, that single, wrong number in the previous porter’s record, was a crack in it. I didn’t need to know *why* it was wrong, not yet. I just needed to see it. 

The way Haro moved, the way he seemed to *know* before he even looked, it reminded me of… nothing good. It reminded me of Cradle. That relentless, grinding need to follow the rules, to understand the system, even when it was actively trying to mislead you. 

I kept reading.
